name: Reentrancy
description: An external call can re-enter a function before its state effects are committed, allowing repeated withdrawals or inconsistent accounting.
root_cause: Interaction with untrusted code occurs before checks and state updates, or a shared lock is missing.
evidence_points: A fallback or receive function can call back into the target contract during an external call.
Checks-effects-interactions places validation first, state effects second, and external calls last.
A reentrancy guard can serialize entry across functions that share the same invariant.
Pull-payment designs reduce the amount of trusted code executed during a withdrawal.
Read-only reentrancy can expose transient state to a view used by another protocol.

name: Broken access control
description: A privileged operation is callable by an unintended account or role, enabling unauthorized minting, withdrawals, upgrades, or configuration changes.
root_cause: Missing, incorrect, or bypassable authorization checks on state-changing entry points.
evidence_points: Every privileged function should enforce the intended caller or role at the contract boundary.
An ownership transfer must validate the new owner and avoid leaving an unusable zero address.
Role administration should be explicit; a role that grants itself can become a privilege-escalation path.
Initialization functions need one-time protection in upgradeable deployments.
Tests should exercise unauthorized callers as well as the expected administrator.

name: Unsafe delegatecall
description: delegatecall executes another contract's code with the caller's storage, balance, and address context; an untrusted target can overwrite critical state.
root_cause: Implementation or target addresses are user-controlled, insufficiently validated, or storage layouts are incompatible.
evidence_points: delegatecall preserves msg.sender and writes to the caller's storage slots.
A user-controlled implementation address can execute arbitrary logic in the caller context.
Proxy implementations need an upgrade authorization boundary and compatibility checks.
Storage slot collisions can corrupt ownership or balances even when the target is trusted.
Use static allowlists or audited proxy patterns instead of forwarding arbitrary calldata.

name: Oracle and price manipulation
description: A protocol trusts a manipulable spot price or stale feed, allowing an attacker to borrow, liquidate, or exchange at an incorrect valuation.
root_cause: Insufficient liquidity, a single-block price source, missing freshness checks, or incorrect feed decimal handling.
evidence_points: A low-liquidity pool's instantaneous reserve ratio can be moved within one transaction.
Time-weighted prices make a manipulation more expensive but do not remove all oracle risk.
Consumers should check the feed round and updated timestamp before using a value.
Feed decimals must be normalized before comparing assets with different units.
A circuit breaker or bounded deviation can limit damage when a feed is unavailable or abnormal.

name: tx.origin authorization
description: Using tx.origin for authorization lets a malicious intermediary contract trick a user into triggering a privileged action.
root_cause: Authorization compares the entire transaction's originator instead of the immediate caller.
evidence_points: tx.origin is the externally owned account that started the transaction, not the immediate caller.
A phishing contract can call a victim contract while preserving the user's tx.origin.
msg.sender identifies the immediate caller and is the usual primitive for access checks.
Meta-transaction systems need an explicit trusted forwarder model rather than tx.origin.
Solidity security guidance recommends never using tx.origin for authorization.

name: Unchecked low-level call result
description: Ignoring the boolean result of call, send, or delegatecall can make a contract continue after an external operation failed.
root_cause: Low-level calls return success data instead of automatically reverting, and the result is not checked.
evidence_points: address.call returns a success flag and returned bytes; it does not throw for every failure.
A failed payment followed by a state update can create insolvency or accounting drift.
Using a checked wrapper such as SafeERC20 makes non-standard token failures explicit.
If failure is acceptable, the code should record and handle it deliberately.
Tests should cover both revert and false-returning callee behavior.

name: Block timestamp dependence
description: Contract logic treats block.timestamp as an exact clock or random value even though block producers have limited influence over it.
root_cause: Time-sensitive or entropy-sensitive decisions rely on a miner/validator-controlled timestamp without tolerance.
evidence_points: block.timestamp is useful for coarse expiries but should not be treated as exact wall-clock time.
A producer may adjust a timestamp within consensus validity bounds.
Short windows and boundary conditions can make timestamp influence economically relevant.
Use block numbers or an oracle when the application needs a different time model.
Avoid using timestamp alone as a source of unpredictable randomness.

name: Weak on-chain randomness
description: Values derived from public block data or predictable state can be anticipated or biased by users and block producers.
root_cause: Unpredictable outcomes use blockhash, timestamp, sender, or similar public inputs without a commit-reveal or oracle.
evidence_points: Block timestamps and hashes are visible to participants and are not secret randomness.
The blockhash for the current block is unavailable during execution and recent hashes have limited history.
Commit-reveal separates choosing a secret from revealing it and can reduce last-mover bias.
A verifiable randomness service supplies a proof that consumers can verify on-chain.
Randomness designs need an explicit response to non-reveal and liveness griefing.

name: Signature replay
description: A valid signed message can be reused in another context, chain, contract, or time because the signed domain lacks replay protection.
root_cause: Messages omit a nonce, chain identifier, verifying contract, expiry, or consume-once state.
evidence_points: A per-signer nonce makes each authorization single-use when the contract consumes it.
EIP-712 domain separation binds typed data to a chain and verifying contract.
Chain IDs can change or fork, so domain handling must follow the chosen signing standard.
Deadlines bound how long an off-chain signature remains valid.
A signature check proves authorization of the message, not that the requested state is still safe.

name: Governance capture
description: Voting power can be temporarily borrowed, concentrated, or exercised without enough delay or quorum to pass harmful proposals.
root_cause: Voting snapshots, delegation, quorum, timelocks, or proposer protections do not match the threat model.
evidence_points: Current-balance voting lets tokens acquired immediately before a vote influence that vote.
Snapshot voting records voting power at a defined block or proposal checkpoint.
A quorum requirement prevents a tiny turnout from controlling a large treasury.
Timelocks give users time to exit or guardians time to cancel a malicious action.
Delegation and vote counting must avoid double counting and handle token transfers consistently.

name: Denial of service from unbounded work
description: A loop or batch operation grows with user-controlled state until it exceeds the block gas limit or becomes impractical to execute.
root_cause: On-chain work scales linearly with an unbounded array, list, or number of recipients.
evidence_points: Block gas limits bound how much computation a transaction can perform.
An attacker can sometimes add entries that force a later loop to exceed the limit.
Pagination lets callers process bounded ranges across multiple transactions.
Pull-based claims avoid one transaction iterating over every recipient.
Gas measurements should include worst-case state size, not only a small fixture.

name: Denial of service by failed external call
description: A loop or state transition reverts when one recipient rejects a call, blocking unrelated users or all progress.
root_cause: The design requires every external payment or callback to succeed before state can advance.
evidence_points: A recipient contract can deliberately revert in its fallback or receive function.
Pushing funds to many recipients couples their liveness to one transaction.
Pull payments let each recipient withdraw independently and handle its own failure.
Skipping a failed recipient must preserve accounting and provide a retry path.
External callbacks should be treated as untrusted and bounded in both gas and effects.

name: Unprotected proxy upgrade
description: An unauthorized account can change a proxy implementation or initializer, replacing trusted behavior with malicious code.
root_cause: Upgrade authorization is missing, incorrectly wired, or the implementation can be initialized by anyone.
evidence_points: The proxy address stays constant while calls execute code at the implementation address.
UUPS implementations must override _authorizeUpgrade with an access restriction.
An upgrade admin should be separated from ordinary user calls according to the proxy pattern.
Initializer functions need one-time guards because constructors do not run in proxy storage.
Upgrade reviews should check storage layout compatibility and the new implementation's permissions.

name: Unsafe token transfer assumptions
description: A contract assumes every ERC-20 transfer returns true or transfers the requested amount, which is false for some tokens and fee-on-transfer designs.
root_cause: Integration relies on optional return data or nominal amounts without checking actual balance changes.
evidence_points: The original ERC-20 ecosystem includes tokens that return no boolean value from transfer.
SafeERC20 treats no return data as success and decodes an explicit false as failure.
Fee-on-transfer tokens may deliver less than the amount requested.
Accounting should use the actual received amount where token behavior permits it.
Approval updates can have race considerations; increase/decrease patterns are safer for some tokens.

name: Rounding and precision errors
description: Integer division truncates values and repeated conversions can accumulate a favorable bias that drains or misprices a system.
root_cause: The order of multiplication and division, scale factors, or rounding direction is not specified for each invariant.
evidence_points: Solidity integer division truncates toward zero and discards a remainder.
Multiplying before dividing preserves precision when the intermediate value cannot overflow.
Rounding direction should favor the protocol or user according to the invariant.
Decimals are metadata; token arithmetic still uses integer base units.
Property tests should cover tiny deposits, withdrawals, and values near conversion boundaries.

name: Frontrunning and transaction-order dependence
description: A pending transaction reveals a price, order, or action that another participant can observe and execute first, changing its outcome.
root_cause: Sensitive operations are public before settlement and have no slippage bound, commit-reveal, or deadline.
evidence_points: Pending transactions may be observed before inclusion and reordered by block builders.
A minimum-output or maximum-input bound limits unexpected execution price movement.
Deadlines prevent stale orders from being executed much later than intended.
Commit-reveal hides order details until a later reveal transaction.
Private order flow changes visibility but does not replace contract-level slippage checks.

name: Arithmetic overflow in pre-0.8 Solidity
description: For Solidity versions before 0.8.0, arithmetic on uint and int wraps silently unless guarded by a checked library or explicit bounds.
root_cause: Legacy compiler semantics allow values to wrap at the type modulus.
evidence_points: Solidity 0.8.0 and later revert on overflow and underflow in ordinary arithmetic.
Unchecked blocks in modern Solidity intentionally restore wrapping behavior for selected operations.
Legacy contracts may use SafeMath to add checks where the compiler does not provide them.
Casting to a smaller integer type can still truncate or revert depending on the operation and version.
Audit conclusions must record the compiler version and enabled optimizer/settings.

name: Proxy storage collision
description: Proxy and implementation variables map to the same storage slots, so an upgrade or delegatecall writes one value over another.
root_cause: Incompatible storage layout, manual slot mistakes, or an unstructured proxy that does not reserve implementation/admin slots.
evidence_points: delegatecall uses the proxy's storage, so implementation variable ordering matters.
Adding variables in the middle of an upgradeable contract can shift later slots.
Append-only storage layout is the usual compatibility rule for upgrades.
Namespaced or standardized slots reduce collisions for proxy metadata.
Upgrade tooling can compare layouts before deployment, but custom assembly still needs review.
